```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE)
options(scipen = 999)
fmt_n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
fmt_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * x)
```

```{r import-and-audit, include=FALSE}
# The CSV retains the spreadsheet's two header rows. The second contains names.
credit_raw <- read.csv(
  "credit_card_default.csv", skip = 1, check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = c("", "NA")
)
pay_cols <- c("PAY_0", paste0("PAY_", 2:6))
bill_cols <- paste0("BILL_AMT", 1:6)
amount_cols <- paste0("PAY_AMT", 1:6)
expected_names <- c(
  "ID", "LIMIT_BAL", "SEX", "EDUCATION", "MARRIAGE", "AGE",
  pay_cols, bill_cols, amount_cols, "default payment next month"
)
stopifnot(identical(names(credit_raw), expected_names))
names(credit_raw)[25] <- "default"

stopifnot(
  nrow(credit_raw) == 30000L,
  all(vapply(credit_raw, is.numeric, logical(1))),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(credit_raw))),
  !anyDuplicated(credit_raw$ID),
  all(credit_raw$default %in% 0:1),
  all(credit_raw$SEX %in% 1:2),
  all(credit_raw$EDUCATION %in% 0:6),
  all(credit_raw$MARRIAGE %in% 0:3),
  all(as.matrix(credit_raw[pay_cols]) %in% -2:9),
  all(credit_raw$LIMIT_BAL > 0),
  all(credit_raw$AGE > 0),
  all(as.matrix(credit_raw[amount_cols]) >= 0)
)

n_clients <- nrow(credit_raw)
n_defaults <- sum(credit_raw$default)
default_rate <- mean(credit_raw$default)
n_identical_records <- sum(duplicated(credit_raw[setdiff(names(credit_raw), "ID")]))
n_negative_bills <- sum(rowSums(credit_raw[bill_cols] < 0) > 0)
n_over_limit <- sum(rowSums(
  sweep(as.matrix(credit_raw[bill_cols]), 1, credit_raw$LIMIT_BAL, ">")
) > 0)
```

# Introduction

Two customers with similar credit limits may have very different repayment histories. One may consistently
make payments, while the other falls behind. This project examines whether those differences
help explain who defaults in the following month, and whether recent financial behavior can provide
more predictive information than demographic characteristics.

We use the "Default of Credit Card Clients" dataset from the [UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/350/default+of+credit+card+clients) ([dataset DOI](https://doi.org/10.24432/C55S3H)). The records concern credit card clients in Taiwan, with monthly histories from April through September 2005. Our local file, `credit_card_default.csv`, is a CSV conversion of the source spreadsheet. It contains `r fmt_n(n_clients)` clients, 23 predictors, an identifier, and a binary response indicating default in the following month. Financial amounts are recorded in New Taiwan dollars (NT$).

When looking through the predictors, we chose to group them into 4 rough categories:

| Group | Original variables | Description |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Customer characteristics | `SEX`, `EDUCATION`, `MARRIAGE`, `AGE` | Recorded sex, education, marital status, and age |
| Credit limit | `LIMIT_BAL` | Amount of credit granted |
| Repayment status | `PAY_0`, `PAY_2` through `PAY_6` | Monthly payment status codes from September back to April |
| Bills and payments | `BILL_AMT1` through `BILL_AMT6`; `PAY_AMT1` through `PAY_AMT6` | Monthly statement balances and payment amounts from September back to April |

Each row in the dataset represents one client, with six monthly observations stored in different variables 
for a particular client (record). In the supplied file, `r fmt_n(n_defaults)` clients 
(`r fmt_pct(default_rate)`) defaulted. From this, we can see that class imbalance exists between the defaulting vs. 
non-defaulting clients.

We propose four related research questions:

1. How is the frequency and recency of recorded payment delays associated with defaulting?

- Compare default rates across repayment histories and use logistic regression to estimate associations while accounting for credit limit and customer characteristics.

2. How much predictive information do financial variables provide beyond demographics, and vice versa?

- Compare demographic only, financial only, and combined models on the same validation folds. 
We can use financial predictors  include credit limit, repayment status, bills, and payments.

3. Does the association between balance relative to credit limit and default differ by recent repayment status?

- Examine interaction between September's bill to limit ratio and September's repayment status (should consider nonlinear model here maybe)

4. Can clients be grouped by their observed financial behavior, and do those groups have different default rates?

- Clustering using financial predictors only, then compare default rates across the resulting groups.


# Data Preprocessing

## Import and data quality

The CSV preserves two spreadsheet header rows: a row of generic labels (`X1` through `X23` and `Y`) followed 
by the descriptive variable names. We skip the first row when importing, rename the response variable to `default`, 
and keep its numeric coding of 0 and 1. We retain the original import as `credit_raw` and 
create a separate analysis dataset, `credit`.

```{r}
audit <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Client records", "Original columns, including ID and response",
            "Missing cells", "Repeated IDs", "Defaults",
            "Repeated records after excluding ID"),
  Result = c(fmt_n(n_clients), ncol(credit_raw), sum(is.na(credit_raw)),
             sum(duplicated(credit_raw$ID)), fmt_n(n_defaults),
             n_identical_records)
)
knitr::kable(audit, align = c("l", "r"))
```

Since there aren't any missing cells or rows with duplicate IDs, we don't need to remote or impute any values.
There are `r n_identical_records` repeated records after excluding ID, but these have distinct identifiers, so
we assume that this is coincidental and not a data entry error with duplicate records. We decided to keep them and
check sensitivity to repeated predictor profiles later during model evaluation for some of the research questions
above. The client ID is kept separately and not used as a predictor.

## Categorical variables

Sex, education, and marital status are treated as categorical rather than numerical variables. The documentation 
from the UCI repository defines education codes 1 - 4 and marital-status codes 1 - 3, but the CSV also includes education 
codes 0, 5, and 6 along with marital status code 0. Since these other undocumented codes could have some predictive power,
we chose to re-label them as a new `Unknown` categories instead of the existing `Other` categories.

```{r}
client_id <- credit_raw$ID
credit <- credit_raw[setdiff(names(credit_raw), "ID")]
credit$SEX <- factor(credit$SEX, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female"))
credit$EDUCATION <- factor(
  ifelse(credit$EDUCATION %in% c(0, 5, 6), 0, credit$EDUCATION),
  levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 0),
  labels = c("Graduate school", "University", "High school", "Other", "Unknown")
)
credit$MARRIAGE <- factor(
  credit$MARRIAGE, levels = c(1, 2, 3, 0),
  labels = c("Married", "Single", "Other", "Unknown")
)

# transform
for (nm in pay_cols) credit[[nm]] <- factor(credit_raw[[nm]])
```

```{r}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Variable = c("Education", "Marital status"),
  `Codes labeled Unknown` = c("0, 5, 6", "0"),
  Clients = c(sum(credit$EDUCATION == "Unknown"),
              sum(credit$MARRIAGE == "Unknown")),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

Repayment codes require particular care. UCI defines -1 as payment made duly and positive values as months of 
delay, but the original source doesn't explain values of -2 or 0. We keep these as separate levels in their own
right rather than treating them as missing, assigning them a meaning, or averaging them with delay lengths. 
For summary features, a recorded delay means a strictly positive status code.

## Financial values and derived predictors

Credit limits are positive and payment amounts are non-negative. However, `r fmt_n(n_negative_bills)` clients 
have at least one negative statement balance, and `r fmt_n(n_over_limit)` have at least one statement 
balance above their recorded credit limit. We chose to treat clients with these values as
valid since the documentation didn't explicitly state that such records are erroneous. For instance,
a statement balance over the credit limit could just mean that the client's credit limit decreased to its 
current amount at some point. We also avoid automatically trimming large balances or payments, since those 
observations may be relevant to default risk.

To connect the data to our questions, we add four summaries while preserving all 23 original predictors:

```{r}
credit$delay_months <- rowSums(credit_raw[pay_cols] > 0)
credit$bill_to_limit_sep <- credit_raw$BILL_AMT1 / credit_raw$LIMIT_BAL
credit$mean_bill_to_limit <- rowMeans(credit_raw[bill_cols]) / credit_raw$LIMIT_BAL
credit$mean_payment_to_limit <- rowMeans(credit_raw[amount_cols]) / credit_raw$LIMIT_BAL

demographic_predictors <- c("SEX", "EDUCATION", "MARRIAGE", "AGE")
financial_predictors <- c("LIMIT_BAL", pay_cols, bill_cols, amount_cols)
cluster_predictors <- c("delay_months", "mean_bill_to_limit", "mean_payment_to_limit")

stopifnot(
  nrow(credit) == n_clients, ncol(credit) == 28L,
  !anyNA(credit), !"ID" %in% names(credit),
  all(credit$delay_months %in% 0:6),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(credit[c(
    "bill_to_limit_sep", "mean_bill_to_limit", "mean_payment_to_limit"
  )])))
)
```

| Derived variable | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| `delay_months` | Number of months with a positive repayment status code (0 - 6). Summarizes the frequency of recorded delays |
| `bill_to_limit_sep` | September statement balance divided by credit limit. Used with September repayment status for the interaction question |
| `mean_bill_to_limit` | Mean of the six statement balances divided by credit limit. Summarizes relative balances |
| `mean_payment_to_limit` | Mean of the six payment amounts divided by credit limit. Summarizes relative payment amounts |

The bill-to-limit ratios can be used as proxies for credit use based on statement balances, and we 
chose to keep negative ratios and ratios > 1. 

We chose to create `mean_payment_to_limit` to avoid the case where payment to bill ratios could be undefined
when bills are 0.

## Notes (delete this later when you add on)

- Remember to use K-fold CV for model selection and to pick the hyperparameters
- If any numeric variables that are associated w/ money are transformed for any of the 
research questions, make sure to use `log1p` for non-negative values and a sign-preserving
function for anything with a negative value.
- Class imbalance exists between defaulting vs. non-defaulting
  - use ROC/AUC and either F-score, balanced accuracy or some other method that takes this into 
  account when evaluating models
- If any of you choose to use clustering MAKE SURE you can vouch that the clustering is good before
attempting to perform any analysis on how the clusters are different w.r.t. each other and the response 
(default rate, etc.)
  - probably dont want to use too many vars since we run into curse of dimensionality
